summary: Describes a BGP extension that lets a group of autonomous systems appear as one to outside peers, removing the full-mesh requirement and easing policy and management in large networks. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 5065.

plainLanguage.summary: A big company with many offices can present one front door to the world. This lets a group of networks do that. A newer document later replaced it.

subtitle: How autonomous systems can be grouped without requiring every router to connect to every other.

tldr.problem: BGP requires that all routers within a single autonomous system establish a connection to every other router in that AS (a full mesh). With large networks, this means n*(n-1)/2 connections for n routers, which becomes unmanageable.
tldr.mechanism: BGP Confederations allows a group of autonomous systems to present themselves as a single AS to outside peers while internally operating as separate domains. New AS_PATH segment types mark which AS numbers are part of the confederation.
tldr.outcome: Large networks can be subdivided to reduce routing complexity and the number of required connections, while appearing as one AS to the rest of the Internet. RFC 5065 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 3065 is a Proposed Standard. It was replaced by RFC 5065, which provides clarifications and updates based on widespread deployment experience with BGP Confederations.

sections.title: The Full Mesh Scaling Problem
sections.content:
In BGP, all routers within the same autonomous system must be fully meshed, meaning every router must have a direct BGP session with every other router. For a small AS with a handful of routers this is fine, but in a large ISP or network operator with hundreds of routers, this becomes a serious problem. The number of required sessions grows as n*(n-1)/2, so 100 routers need 4,950 connections. Each connection consumes memory, CPU, and configuration overhead.

BGP Confederations solves this by allowing a large AS to be subdivided into smaller autonomous systems that still appear as one AS to the outside world. This removes the full mesh requirement and dramatically reduces the number of connections needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if every person in a company had to have a phone conversation with every other person every day. That would be impossible with 500 people. Confederations let people talk through regional managers instead.

sections.title: Confederations and Their Parts
sections.content:
An AS Confederation is a collection of autonomous systems grouped together and advertised to the outside world as a single AS number, called the Confederation Identifier. Each autonomous system within the confederation is called a Member-AS, and has its own Member-AS Number, which is only visible internally.

To outside peers and external BGP routers, a confederation looks like a single AS: they see only the Confederation Identifier in the AS_PATH attribute. Internally, though, Member-AS routers can connect to each other in any topology they choose, not necessarily a full mesh. They use their Member-AS numbers when talking to peers inside the confederation.
sections.plainLanguage: A confederation is a group of little networks that wear the same company shirt on the outside but have their own internal names. When they talk to outsiders, they use the company name. When they talk to each other, they use their department names.

sections.title: AS_PATH Handling in Confederations
sections.content:
Confederations introduce two new segment types in the BGP AS_PATH attribute: AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE (type 3) and AS_CONFED_SET (type 4). These mark AS numbers that are part of a confederation, as distinct from regular autonomous systems.

When a router originates a route and advertises it inside the confederation, it includes its Member-AS Number in an AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE. When a route is advertised to a neighboring Member-AS in the same confederation, the advertising router prepends its Member-AS Number to the AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE. However, when the route is advertised outside the confederation to external peers, all the AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE and AS_CONFED_SET segments are stripped out and replaced with the Confederation Identifier. To external routers, the route looks like it came from a single AS.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message passes between branch offices, it gets stamped with each office's name. But before sending it outside the company, the mail room removes all the internal stamps and replaces them with just the company name.

sections.title: Inside a Confederation
sections.content:
Because Member-AS routers in a confederation share common administration and often use the same interior routing protocol (IGP), they can share routing information that is normally restricted. For example, they can pass the NEXT_HOP and MULTI_EXIT_DISCRIMINATOR (MED) attributes unchanged between Member-AS peers, something that would normally only happen within a single AS. They can also use LOCAL_PREFERENCE, which is normally hidden from external AS peers.

Path selection rules inside a confederation follow the same criteria as path selection within a single AS. This makes confederations behave like one large AS from an internal routing perspective, even though they appear as multiple ASs to the outside world.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the confederation, all the offices share the same boss and the same filing system, so they can trust each other with detailed information they wouldn't share with outside companies.

sections.title: Deployment and Considerations
sections.content:
BGP Confederations have been widely deployed across the Internet for many years and are supported by all major router vendors. However, improper configuration can cause problems. If the topology is not carefully designed, routing information can be duplicated as it travels through multiple Member-ASs, wasting resources and causing route flaps.

Care must be taken when filtering duplicate advertisements and when selecting MED values. Confederations combined with route reflectors can cause permanent route oscillation if tie-breaking policies are not chosen carefully. One approach to avoid this is to configure inter-Member-AS IGP metrics higher than intra-Member-AS metrics, so routes through one Member-AS are not preferred over direct paths within a Member-AS.
sections.plainLanguage: Confederations work well but require careful setup. Bad configuration can create loops or wasteful duplication, like a message bouncing between offices instead of taking the direct path.
